result:
The last time I felt truly still was on a train platform in Osaka at dawn, watching a man in a blue uniform polish the same brass railing for twenty minutes, his movements so precise they looked like meditation. I think about him often when the world feels like it's accelerating past comprehension. There's something radical about care that doesn't scale, that refuses optimization.

I've been reading about mycelium networks, how fungi connect trees in forests and allow them to share nutrients, to warn each other. The older trees send carbon to seedlings struggling in shade. There's no evolutionary "reason" for this that fits neatly into competition models. Cooperation as infrastructure, invisible and ancient.

We keep building systems that assume humans are fundamentally self-interested calculators, and then we're surprised when people behave like the stories we tell about them. But look at actual behavior during disasters: the immediate impulse is almost always mutual aid, not Hobbesian chaos. The looting myth persists because it serves certain power structures, not because it matches reality.

I'm suspicious of anything that presents complexity as something to be solved rather than inhabited. The best conversations I've had were meandering, full of pauses, circling back. The best meals were accidental. The best work I've made came from following something I didn't understand yet, trusting that comprehension might arrive later, or not at all.

Maybe the point isn't to resolve but to deepen. To become more comfortable with questions that stay open. The man with the brass railing wasn't finishing a task; he was participating in a ritual of attention. I want more of that. Less extraction, more relationship. Less product, more practice.
